[prose] The geographic extent of bioclimatic variables to model current distribution covered northern Morocco, the Iberian Peninsula and southern France, between latitudes 30 N and $$4 5 ^ { \circ }$ N,$ and longitudes $1 0 ^ { \circ }$ W and $$5 ^ { \circ }$ 巨 .$ The predictions of future potential distribution were exclusively limited to the Iberian Peninsula and South of France. Current climatic conditions were described by 19 bioclimatic variables based on temperature and rainfall values. These variables were downloaded from [worldclim.org](http://worldclim.org) at 30 arc-second resolution based on monthly averages for the period 1970–2000. Bioclimatic variables are commonly used in SDMs for predicting species ranges and were originally created to generate more biologically meaningful variables than traditional environmental metrics such as mean temperature and pre-cipitation (O’Donnell & Ignizio, 2012).

[prose] The thermal sensitivity of odonates drives species distribution and turnover along the latitudinal gradient and makes them a potential indicator for environmental change (Dingemanse & Kalkman, 2008; Hassall et al., 2007; Rocha-Ortega et al., 2020). Concurrently with climate warming in Central and Northern Europe, a clear trend of rapid northward range expansion of odonates has been observed (Markovic et al., 2014; Termaat et al., 2019). For instance, at least 15 Mediterranean species have expanded their geographic range to Central and Northern Europe since 2009, whereas some African species have expanded to Southern Europe (Ott, 2010). In the Iberian Peninsula, at least six African species have arrived from Morocco during the last 60 years and are currently experiencing northward expansion. Climate warming may also be changing the phenology of odonates; for instance, an earlier beginning and a prolongation of the flight season have been recorded (Dingemanse & Kalkman, 2008; Richter et al., 2008).

Species categorised as either ‘Expanded’ or ‘Displaced’ lived preferentially in eutrophic waters in lowlands and/or in middle-mountain and their habitat preferences were mostly ponds, wetlands and pools. Within the ‘Expanded’ category, most species did not have egg diapause, showed multivoltinism and the upper limit of their distribution was the Iberian Peninsula (species expanded from North Africa), whereas species within the category ‘Displaced’ were characterised by univoltinism, their flight season was in summer and the Iberian Peninsula was their central and lower distribution limit (Mediterranean species). Most species in the category ‘Reduced and displaced’ were widely distributed in the Iberian Peninsula, lived in streams and rivers in lowlands and at middle elevations and were univoltines. Finally, species in the category ‘Reduced’ lived in oligotrophic waters in mountain lakes, ponds and pools, the Iberian Peninsula was the lower limit of their distribution (species mainly distributed in Central Europe), and showed semivoltinism and a diapause period.

[prose] The modelled future climate in the Iberian Peninsula will be characterised by both warming and increased seasonality, which should likely involve a higher frequency of droughts, as previously reported (Giorgi & Lionello, 2008; Valdes-Abellan et al., 2017). As a consequence, our SDMs anticipated changes in the distribution of suitable habitats for all Odonata species, clustering species into distinct rangeshift categories. The ‘Expanded’ and ‘Reduced and displaced’ were the two most common responses. Based on the functional space generated, the distinct range-shift categories were most strongly associated to larval development rate, the duration of flight season, permanence of the preferred habitat type and oviposition habitat. Moreover, the three biogeographic origins, North Africa, the Mediterranean basin and Central Europe (Torralba-Burrial & Ocharan Larrondo, 2007), also discriminated among categories. Central European species were mainly clustered in the ‘Reduced and displaced’ category, whereas the North African and Mediterranean species were categorised as ‘Expanded’. All traits studied and the range-shift categories were decoupled from the phylogenetic relatedness between species, which rejects phylogenetic trait conservatism and reveals that the phylogenetic relatedness of odonates cannot anticipate a range-shift category, in contrast with results found for plants (Davis et al., 2010; Fei et al., 2017). Hence, future biodiversity conservation plans for facing climate change of odonates should be based on functional traits rather than on lineage identity, as illustrated by the opposite responses found across the closely related Aeshna species (Figure 3).

The trait categories most correlated to the first axis were semivoltinism (NC0) together with the opposite patterns of behaviour fliers (FBF) versus perchers (FBP), and the water quality oligotrophic (WO) versus eutrophic (WE). The second axis was mostly related with the opposite directions of absence (DN) versus presence (DY) of egg diapause. The trait categories most correlated with axes (>0.6) were selected (Supporting information S9).

[prose] 1. Climate change has the potential to modify habitat characteristics and, consequently, induce species responses to ongoing environmental changes. Functional traits determine both if a species can persist and maintain stable population sizes in particular ecological conditions, and its capacity to disperse to more favourable habitats. 2. Given that functional traits evolve over time, one could expect closely related species to show similar responses to climate change, which should identify vulnerable lineages. Alternatively, species-specific functional traits may anticipate species responses to climate change, and therefore, trait composition should be a strong predictor. 3. We compiled a comprehensive dataset of functional traits of 84 Iberian and Moroccan odonates species and built a phylogenetic tree to determine if dissimilarity of traits and phylogenetic relatedness are relevant to better discriminate species range-shift responses to climate change. 4. Modelling results for 66 species showed clear impacts of the increase in temperature and drought events on their potential distribution. [prose] Among freshwater macroinvertebrates, Odonata (Insecta) are a good model taxon for exploring the effects of climate warming on freshwater biodiversity because (1) they originated in the tropics, which implies tolerance to high temperatures; (2) adults present high morphological differentiation across species, which facilitates capture, identification and recording; (3) they occur with medium to high local abundances and are present in almost all freshwater habitats, with high species turnover due to larval and adult preferences in habitat use and evident niche partition among species; (4) they present high phenotypic variability, both within and between species, in traits pre-sumably involved in adaptation to climate warming, such as emergence and duration of flight season; and (5) there is a large and wellknown body of historical research, including extensive recording and rich historical datasets from citizen science projects (Corser et al., 2014; Hassall & Thompson, 2008; Termaat et al., 2019).

[prose] To determine the current species distribution, binary logistic generalised linear models (GLM) and boosted regression trees (BRT) were run for each species because testing for several algorithms is suggested to optimise the predictions for each particular species (Konowalik & Nosol, 2021; Qiao et al., 2015). GLM represents a flexible extension of linear models that allows for response variables that have a non-normal distribution error (binomial in the case of binary responses), whereas BRT combines regression trees for generating large numbers of simple distribution models that are selected for the best prediction by boosting algorithms (Elith et al., 2008; Franklin, 2010; Kienast et al., 2012). To create the input SDM matrix, the current bioclimatic information was extracted for each spatial point. The database created for each species was split into 70% as training set and 30% as testing set by random partition to validate the models. Each model was evaluated independently by three predictors of significance to select the model with the best performance: (1) by means of area under curve (AUC) statistics from a receiver-operating characteristic analysis (ROC), which is a threshold-independent evaluation of model discrimination (Fielding & Bell, 1997); (2) by true skills statistics (TSS), which is a measure of accuracy (Allouche et al., 2006) and (3) by odds ratio skill score (ORSS), which measures skill compared to a random prediction (Stephenson, 2000). AUC and TSS were the two metrics that achieved the highest performance compared to other evaluation models (Konowalik & Nosol, 2021) (Supporting information S2). The widely used logistic regression (fitted with GLM) was selected for the majority of species. However, for some species that had low numbers of occurrences (fewer than 70 grid cells), the BRT models (learning $\mathsf { r a t e } = 0 . 0 0 1$ , bag fraction = 0.75) performed better than GLM, as previously suggested (Konowalik & Nosol, 2021). All models were performed and evaluated using the R software (R Core Team, 2016) and the package ‘gbm (Ridgeway et al., 2015).

[prose] The final dataset included 84 Odonata species and 75,767 individual recorded presences. In general, the selected bioclimatic variables showed an increase in both average temperature and temperature seasonality and a decrease in mean temperature of the wettest quarter and total precipitation and precipitation seasonality by 2050. SDMs were run for 66 out of 84 species analysed. Besides the 10 species initially removed, another four species were discarded because were rare and locally distributed, for example, Cordulegaster bidentata was recorded in only 30 nearby grid cells. The selected SDM was logistic regression for 60 species, whereas BRT was selected for 7 species (Supporting information S2). Of the five selected variables, the most used variables for modelling distribution were Bio 4 (Temperature seasonality) and Bio 15 (Precipitation seasonality), while the less utilised variable was Bio 3 (Isothermality). The model evaluation showed high correlation $( R ^ { 2 }$ > 0.90) among the indices used (Supporting information S2). In general, all values of AUC were higher than 0.6 and commonly higher than 0.7, which means all predictive models are robust and reliable.

After eliminating the trait with the least discriminating power, the procedure was repeated until all traits that were left in the discriminant analysis were significant. We note that this variable selection procedure produces a parsimonious model, but does not imply that traits not selected in the final model carry no discriminating power: all the usual caveats about automatic variable selection apply here too. We run twice the analyses to compare the robustness of the results, once using all species and again with the subset of species for which the models performed well (AUC > 0.6). The results were consistent (Supporting information S2), and only results including all species are discussed.
